facts.title: The Last Stable Element Found
facts.text: Rhenium was the last element with a stable isotope to be discovered, identified in 1925 by German chemists Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, and Otto Berg using X-ray spectroscopy. To isolate their first gram, they had to process around 660 kilograms of the ore molybdenite. Its position had long been predicted by Mendeleev, who called the missing element 'dvi-manganese'.

facts.title: Named After a River
facts.text: The element's name comes from the Latin 'Rhenus', meaning the Rhine, the great river that flows through western Germany near where its discoverers worked. This made it a fitting tribute to their homeland. Ida Noddack (born Tacke) is also notable as one of the few women credited with discovering an element.

facts.title: Almost the Highest Melting Point
facts.text: Rhenium melts at about 3186 degrees Celsius, the third highest of any element after tungsten and carbon. It also has one of the highest boiling points of all elements, around 5630 degrees Celsius. This extreme heat resistance is why it stays solid in environments that would vaporize most other metals.

facts.title: Jet Engines Run On It
facts.text: The single largest use of rhenium is in nickel-based superalloys for the turbine blades of jet engines and gas turbines. Adding just 3 to 6 percent rhenium lets blades withstand higher temperatures and resist creep, improving fuel efficiency and engine life. Because of this, a large share of world rhenium production goes into military and commercial aviation.

facts.title: Rarer Than Gold
facts.text: Rhenium is among the rarest elements in Earth's crust, with an abundance of roughly 0.0007 parts per million, making it scarcer than gold or platinum. It is almost never found as its own mineral and has no concentrated ores of its own. Instead, it is recovered as a byproduct of refining molybdenum from copper porphyry deposits, especially in Chile, the United States, and Kazakhstan.

facts.title: A Volcano's Mineral
facts.text: For decades rhenium was known to occur only diffusely scattered in other minerals, never in pure form. Then in 1994 scientists discovered rheniite, a rhenium sulfide mineral, condensing from the scorching fumaroles of the Kudryavy volcano on Iturup Island in Russia's Kuril chain. The volcano belches out an estimated 20 to 60 kilograms of rhenium each year through its volcanic gases.

facts.title: A Cosmic Clock
facts.text: The isotope rhenium-187 slowly decays into osmium-187 with a half-life of about 41.6 billion years, far longer than the age of the universe. Astronomers and geologists use this rhenium-osmium decay as a 'cosmochronometer' to date meteorites and to estimate the age of the elements in our galaxy. The decay is unusual because the emitted electron has so little energy that it is extremely sensitive to the atom's surroundings.

facts.title: A Theranostic Partner
facts.text: Radioactive isotopes of rhenium, especially rhenium-186 and rhenium-188, are used in nuclear medicine to treat cancer and ease bone pain from tumors. Rhenium-188 is convenient because it can be milked from a tungsten-188 generator right in the clinic, much like a familiar technetium generator. Its chemistry closely mirrors that of technetium, making it a natural partner for combined imaging-and-therapy approaches.

facts.title: Catalyst For Cleaner Fuel
facts.text: Rhenium teamed with platinum forms a powerful catalyst used in petroleum refineries to reform naphtha into high-octane, low-lead gasoline. These bimetallic catalysts resist poisoning and last longer than platinum alone. Rhenium compounds also catalyze specialized reactions like olefin metathesis, valued in the chemical industry.

facts.title: It Has No Biological Role
facts.text: Unlike iron or zinc, rhenium plays no known role in any living organism and is not required for life. Because it is so scarce and chemically inert in its metallic form, it is considered to have low toxicity, though detailed safety data remain limited. Researchers are nonetheless exploring designed rhenium complexes as glowing probes that can light up the inside of cells under a microscope.
